domain: Constitutional Law / Political Systems / State Sovereignty
topic_summary: Analysis of the 'One Country, Two Systems' constitutional framework governing Hong Kong post-1997, examining competing interpretations of the Sino-British Joint Declaration and Basic Law kernel. Beijing's sovereignty-primacy reading versus Hong Kong civil society's autonomy-primacy reading emit structurally different constraints on state authority, judicial independence, and civil liberties.

key_entities: People's Republic of China / Central People's Government (sovereign authority; interprets Basic Law via NPCSC)
Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (sub-national entity; claimed autonomous legal system)
Sino-British Joint Declaration 1984 (founding treaty; international registration with UN)
Hong Kong Basic Law (mini-constitution; enacted by PRC National People's Congress 1990)
Hong Kong Judiciary (claimed independent; final interpretation power contested)
Hong Kong Civil Society / Pro-Democracy Movement (claims treaty rights; invokes international law)
key_tensions: Absolute sovereignty (PRC constitutional doctrine) vs treaty-bound autonomy (Joint Declaration obligations)
National security (mainland priority post-2019) vs civil liberties (Basic Law Articles 27-39)
NPCSC interpretive authority (PRC constitutional structure) vs common-law judicial independence (Hong Kong legal tradition)
key_mechanisms: NPCSC Standing Committee interpretations (binding constitutional amendments without HK Legislative Council approval)
National Security Law 2020 (mainland agencies operating in HK; extraterritorial jurisdiction; secret trials)
Chief Executive appointment process (Beijing approval required; democratic nomination effectively eliminated)
key_absences: Enforcement mechanism for Joint Declaration violations (no international arbitration clause; UK has no standing post-handover)
Democratic accountability pathway for Chief Executive selection (universal suffrage 'ultimate aim' never operationalized)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The Sino-British Joint Declaration (1984) and Hong Kong Basic Law (1990) jointly establish 'One Country, Two Systems' as the constitutional framework guaranteeing Hong Kong's capitalist system and way of life for 50 years post-handover (1997-2047)
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Beijing claims interpretive authority through NPCSC Standing Committee (PRC constitutional structure). Hong Kong civil society invokes treaty obligations and international law, but lacks enforcement mechanism post-UK withdrawal.

readings.commitment: One Country, Two Systems means Hong Kong autonomy is delegated by and revocable through PRC sovereign authority; national security and territorial integrity override local autonomy when they conflict
readings.authority_grounding: PRC constitutional hierarchy (NPCSC interpretive supremacy); Westphalian sovereignty doctrine
readings.expected_structural_delta: State coercion enters Hong Kong legal system via National Security Law; mainland enforcement agents operate in HK; political speech/assembly becomes high-epsilon constraint; judiciary loses independence on national security matters

readings.commitment: One Country, Two Systems means Hong Kong retains substantive autonomy with meaningful checks on mainland interference; civil liberties and judicial independence are treaty-guaranteed and internationally enforceable
readings.authority_grounding: International treaty law (Joint Declaration as registered UN treaty); common-law constitutional tradition; democratic legitimacy claims
readings.expected_structural_delta: Mainland intervention is treaty violation; civil liberties remain low-epsilon for most residents; judicial review constrains executive power; democratic reform pathway remains live

readings.commitment: One Country, Two Systems requires substantive negotiation between sovereignty and autonomy; neither absolute; functional division of powers with contested boundaries resolved through political accommodation rather than legal supremacy
readings.authority_grounding: Pragmatic statecraft; historical compromise between incompatible constitutional traditions; de facto power-sharing
readings.expected_structural_delta: Medium-epsilon constraint regime; periodic crises trigger renegotiation; both legal systems acknowledge limits; civil society retains bargaining power through economic/international leverage

axiom_contradictions.basis: Sovereignty primacy holds that delegated autonomy is revocable by sovereign fiat (PRC constitutional supremacy). Autonomy primacy holds that treaty-guaranteed rights create binding legal constraints on sovereign action (international law supremacy). No single coherent framework can hold both: either sovereign authority is absolute and treaties are revocable instruments, or treaties bind sovereigns and create enforceable rights. These are mutually exclusive foundational premises about the source and limits of state authority.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition successfully identified three structurally distinct readings. Sovereignty_primacy and autonomy_primacy readings exhibit axiom contradiction (mutually exclusive foundational premises about state authority). Balanced_coexistence reading represents pragmatic third path that may have collapsed post-2019. Deferred axes capture downstream consequences and structural conditions without redundancy.
